figures.caption: Figure 4: Performance of behavior-based malware detection rules at different LLM deferral thresholds.

Table 4: Comparison of False Negative Rates (FNR) across Rules (with LLM deferral threshold 𝜏 = 6) and gradientboosted decision tree (GBDT) models for families present in (Seen) and not present in (New) the training data. Column 7 shows the percentage ofmalware samples eachmonth from families not in the training data.

Figure 1: The LLM analyzes a malware sample’s behavior report (panel 1) and identifies suspicious behaviors (panel 2). It then formalizes these behaviors into malware detection rules (panel 3). These rules generalize to new malware samples while maintaining low false positive rates (bottom panel).

Figure 5: Performance over time of three different malware detection schemes: a gradient-boosted decision tree trained on EMBER features, behavior-based rules with an LLM deferral threshold of 𝜏 = 6, and Trident, which combines a decision tree, rules, and LLM analysis under a majority vote.

Figure 6: Median behavior report size for true positives and false negatives of the behavior-based detection rules, by sandbox. On every sandbox, false negatives are correlated with much less informative behavior reports.

Figure 7: Behavior-based rules guard against concept drift. This sample, from a family not present in the training data, goes undetected by the gradient-boosted decision tree trained on static EMBER features. However, due to shared behavior with several older malware families, it is detected by multiple behavioral rules.

Figure 8: Comparison of Trident to a gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT) with active learning. Each month, the GBDT model is retrained with an additional 1% of labeled data from the previous month. Trident uses no new labels.

Figure 2: Rules can reduce LLM false positives. The LLM categorizes this sample as malware based on a suspicious behavior in the sandbox report. However, when this behavior is encapsulated in a rule and evaluated, it is proven to occur in small but meaningful percentage of benign samples. Thus, this behavior is not a reliable indicator of maliciousness.
